title: Emerton–Gee stacks, Serre weights, and Breuil–Mézard conjectures for $\mathrm{GSp}_4$
abstract_html: We construct a moduli stack of rank 4 symplectic projective étale \((φ,Γ)\)-modules and prove its geometric properties for any prime \(p>2\) and finite extension \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\). When \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified, we adapt the theory of local models recently developed by Le–Le Hung–Levin–Morra to study the geometry of potentially crystalline substacks in this stack. In particular, we prove the unibranch property at torus fixed points of local models and deduce that tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings are domain under genericity conditions. As applications, we prove, under appropriate genericity conditions, an \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\)-analogue of the Breuil–Mézard conjecture for tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture formulated by Gee–Herzig–Savitt for global Galois representations valued in \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) satisfying Taylor–Wiles conditions, and a modularity lifting result for tamely potentially crystalline representations.
introduction_html:
Background

Serre’s modularity conjecture predicts that every continuous, irreducible, odd Galois representation \(\overline{r}: \mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q}) \rightarrow\mathrm{GL}_2(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p)\) arises from modular forms [ref]. Its refined version predicts the minimal weight of modular forms that give rise to \(\overline{r}\) in terms of the restriction of \(\overline{r}\) at \(p\). The weight part of Serre’s conjecture, saying that the original conjecture implies the refined conjecture, was crucial for the proof of the conjecture due to Kisin and Khare–Winterberger [ref].

The weight part of Serre’s conjecture has been generalized, most notably, to 2-dimensional Galois representations over a totally real field [ref], to Galois representations over a totally real field valued in \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) [ref] and in more general groups \(G\) [ref]. (Both [ref] and [ref] assume that \(p\) is unramified in the totally real field and the Galois representations are tamely ramified at places above \(p\). See [ref] for a generalization to wildly ramified representations, and [ref] for a generalization to a totally real field in which \(p\) ramifies.) In these generalizations, the notion of weight is replaced by Serre weights, namely, isomorphism classes of irreducible \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\)-representations of \(G(\mathbf{F}_q)\).

Although stated in the global context, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture is closely related to the mod \(p\) Langlands program. Let \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) be a finite extension. The mod \(p\) Langlands program predicts a certain correspondence between admissible smooth \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\)-representations of a \(p\)-adic reductive group \(G(K)\) and continuous representations of \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{K}/K)\) valued in its dual group \(G^\vee(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p)\). In this article, we only consider \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\) or \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\), in which case \(G^\vee\) is isomorphic to \(G\). Such a correspondence has been established only in the case \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2\) and \(K=\mathbf{Q}_p\) [ref] or \(G=\mathrm{GL}_1\). Despite many recent advances (for example, see [ref]) in the program, its intricate nature remains poorly understood, and a precise conjecture for \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\) was only made recently [ref] in a categorical language. However, using global methods, one can construct a candidate for a mod \(p\) Langlands correspondence, namely, an admissible smooth \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\)-representation \(\Pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(K)\) associated with an \(n\)-dimensional continuous \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\)-representation \(\overline{\rho}\) of \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{K}/K)\). One major open problem is to prove that \(\Pi\) only depends on \(\overline{\rho}\) and not on non-canonical choices made in the global argument. The weight part of Serre’s conjecture describes the Serre weights appearing in the \(\mathrm{GL}_n({\mathcal{O}}_K)\)-socle of \(\Pi\) explicitly in terms of \(\overline{\rho}|_{I_K}\). Thus, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture has been a guiding principle in the mod \(p\) Langlands program.

The theory of Galois deformations has played an important role in many advances in proving the weight part of Serre’s conjecture ( [ref]), in the mod \(p\) and \(p\)-adic Langlands program ( [ref]), and in proving modularity lifting results ( [ref]). Recently, Emerton–Gee constructed an object that algebraically interpolates deformation spaces of \(n\)-dimensional \(p\)-adic Galois representations (called the Emerton–Gee stack [ref]). The Emerton–Gee stack allows us to employ more geometric methods to study \(p\)-adic Galois representations. More importantly, it is an essential ingredient in formulating the categorical mod \(p\) and \(p\)-adic Langlands conjecture [ref]. When \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified, [ref] developed a theory of local models to study the geometry of potentially crystalline substacks in Emerton–Gee stacks. In particular, it is applied to analyze singularities of tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings. This led to several applications, including the weight part of Serre’s conjecture and the Breuil–Mézard conjecture. The objective of this article is to generalize Emerton–Gee stacks, local models, and their applications to Serre weight conjectures and the Breuil–Mézard conjecture to the group \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\).

Emerton–Gee stacks for \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\)

Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) be a finite extension with the ring of integers \({\mathcal{O}}_K\), a uniformizer \(\varpi\), and the residue field \(k\). We also fix a sufficiently large finite extension \(E/\mathbf{Q}_p\) with the ring of integers \({\mathcal{O}}\), a uniformizer \(\varpi\), and the residue field \(\mathbf{F}\).

In [ref], Emerton–Gee constructed \({\mathcal{X}}_{n,K}\) a moduli stack of rank \(n\) projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules. For a finite \({\mathcal{O}}\)-algebra \(A\), rank \(n\) projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\) modules with \(A\)-coefficients are equivalent to continuous representations of \(G_K:=\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{K}/K)\) on rank \(n\) projective \(A\)-modules. However, for general \(A\), étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules behave better than \(G_K\)-representations in algebraic families. In particular, a family of reducible étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules can converge to an irreducible one, unlike \(G_K\)-representations. Thus, \({\mathcal{X}}_{n,K}\) is considered the correct notion of a moduli stack of “\(p\)-adic Langlands parameters”.

To generalize Emerton–Gee stacks to \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\), we define a symplectic projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-module to be a triple \((M,N,\alpha)\) where \(M\) is a rank 4 projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\) module, \(N\) is a rank 1 projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-module, and \(\alpha: M\simeq M^\vee \otimes N\) is an essentially self-dual isomorphism satisfying a certain sign condition (Definition [•]). These reflect the underlying 4-dimensional vector space of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\), the similitude character of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\), and the non-degenerate skew-symmetric bilinear form on the 4-dimensional vector space, respectively. Under Fontaine’s equivalence, symplectic projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules with \(A\)-coefficients for finite local \({\mathcal{O}}\)-algebra \(A\) are equivalent to continuous representations \(\rho: G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(A)\). We let \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}\) be a category fibered in groupoids over \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spf}}}{\mathcal{O}}\) whose groupoid of \(A\)-points, for a \(p\)-adically complete \({\mathcal{O}}\)-algebra \(A\), is the groupoid of symplectic projective étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules with \(A\)-coefficients. The following Theorem generalizes main properties of \({\mathcal{X}}_{n,K}\) to \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}\).

Theorem 1 (Theorem [•], Proposition [•], Theorem [•]). Suppose that \(p>2\).

  1. The category fibered in groupoids \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}\) is a Noetherian formal algebraic stack.

  2. For each Hodge type \(\lambda\) and inertial type \(\tau\), there exists a closed substack \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}^{\lambda,\tau}\) (resp. \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}^{{\mathrm{ss}},\lambda,\tau}\)) which is a \(p\)-adic formal algebraic stack and flat over \({\mathcal{O}}\). It is uniquely characterized as the \({\mathcal{O}}\)-flat closed substack such that for any finite flat \({\mathcal{O}}\)-algebra \(A\), \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}^{\lambda,\tau}(A)\) (resp. \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}^{{\mathrm{ss}},\lambda,\tau}(A)\)) is equivalent to the groupoid of representations \(\rho:G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(A)\) such that \(\rho\otimes_A E\) is potentially crystalline (resp. semistable) with Hodge type \(\lambda\) and inertial type \(\tau\).

  3. The underlying reduced substack \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{red}}}\subset {\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}\) is an algebraic stack over \(\mathbf{F}\) equidimensional of dimension \(4[K:\mathbf{Q}_p]\). Moreover, its irreducible components are naturally labeled by Serre weights.

The proof of item (1) and (2) use the corresponding results for the Emerton–Gee stack for \(\mathrm{GL}_4\times \mathrm{GL}_1\) and can be easily generalized to \(\mathrm{GSp}_{2n}\). To prove item (3), we first construct irreducible components corresponding to Serre weights and prove that their union equals the stack \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{red}}}\), following the strategy for \(\mathrm{GL}_n\). The construction of irreducible components requires a generalization of a result of Emerton–Gee constructing a family of extensions using abelian Galois cohomology. One difference between \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) and \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) is the presence of a non-abelian unipotent radical of a maximal parabolic subgroup \(Q\) called the Klingen parabolic subgroup. It is unclear how the construction of Emerton–Gee can be generalized to the non-abelian case. Instead, we construct a family of extensions valued in \(Q\) inside a family of extensions valued in the minimal parabolic of \(\mathrm{GL}_4\) containing \(Q\) by only using abelian Galois cohomology. To prove that their union is equal to the stack \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{red}}}\), we need to prove the existence of crystalline lifts for any continuous representation \(G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\). In this case, it seems inevitable to use non-abelian Galois cohomology. We prove this by using the main result in [ref], which develops an obstruction theory for lifting mod \(p\) representations of \(G_K\) valued in reductive groups.

Recently, Zhongyipan Lin constructed a generalization of the Emerton–Gee stack to an arbitrary reductive group proved its Noetherian formal algebraicity using a Tannakian formalism [ref].

Local models for potentially crystalline stacks

Assume that \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified of degree \(f\).

In [ref], the authors constructed local models of potentially crystalline substacks of \({\mathcal{X}}_{n,K}\) using Breuil–Kisin modules. One can associate a Breuil–Kisin module with descent data to a lattice in a potentially crystalline representation. Using this, they identify the potentially crystalline stacks (with bounded \(p\)-adic Hodge type) with a certain closed substack of the moduli stack of Breuil–Kisin modules with descent data constructed in [ref]. It is proved in loc. cit. that the moduli stack of Breuil–Kisin modules with descent data is smoothly equivalent to a Pappas–Zhu local model studied in [ref]. The innovation in [ref] is a construction of certain subvarieties in Pappas–Zhu local models whose open neighborhoods are, after \(p\)-adic completion, smoothly equivalent to open neighborhoods of potentially crystalline stacks.

The Pappas–Zhu local models exist for any connected reductive group which splits over a tamely ramified base change. Let \(M(\le\lambda)\) be the Pappas–Zhu local model over \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}}{\mathcal{O}}\) associated to the group \(\Res_{K/\mathbf{Q}_p}\mathrm{GSp}_4\), Iwahori subgroup of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(K)\), and a regular Hodge type \(\lambda\). Following the idea of [ref], we construct a closed subvariety \(M(\lambda,\nabla_{{\mathbf{a}}_\tau})\subset M(\le\lambda)\) for a tame inertial type \(\tau\) (see Definition [•] and §[•]). It is a projective variety equipped with a natural \(T^f\)-action. Its \(T^f\)-fixed points are given by certain elements \(\widetilde{z}\) in the extended affine Weyl group of \((\mathrm{GSp}_4)^f\). Our main result on the local model is the following.

Theorem 1 (Theorem [•]). Suppose that \(\lambda\) is regular and \(\tau\) is sufficiently generic (depending on \(\lambda\)). Then \(M(\lambda,\nabla_{{\mathbf{a}}_\tau})\) is unibranch at any \(T^f\)-fixed point \(\widetilde{z}\in M(\lambda,\nabla_{{\mathbf{a}}_\tau})(\mathbf{F})\).

Let \({\mathcal{X}}^{\le \lambda,\tau}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{reg}}}\) be the scheme-theoretic union of \({\mathcal{X}}^{\lambda',\tau}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K}\) for \(\lambda'\le \lambda\) regular. For sufficiently generic \(\tau\), the \(p\)-adic completion of the variety \(M(\lambda,\nabla_{{\mathbf{a}}_\tau})\) is locally smoothly equivalent to \({\mathcal{X}}^{\le \lambda,\tau}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{reg}}}\) (Theorem [•]). As a result, Theorem [•] implies the following result on Galois deformation rings. This is the main ingredient for applications below.

Corollary 1. Suppose that \(\lambda\) is regular and \(\tau\) is sufficiently generic (depending on \(\lambda\)). If \(\overline{\rho}: G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\) is tame, then the potentially crystalline deformation ring \(R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\) with Hodge type \(\lambda\) and tame inertial type \(\tau\) is a domain if it is nonzero.

Remark 1. As in [ref], our main results on local models, as well as their applications, hold under suitable genericity conditions, which will be made explicit in the text. In particular, genericity conditions imply that the Hodge type \(\lambda\) is small relative to \(p\). We refer readers to §1.3 in loc. cit. for discussions on genericity conditions.

The inertial local Langlands correspondence

For a mildly generic tame inertial type \(\tau\), we construct an irreducible representation \(\sigma(\tau)\) of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(k)\) in characteristic zero such that if a smooth representation \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(K)\) contains \(\sigma(\tau)\) (viewed as a \(\mathrm{GSp}_4({\mathcal{O}}_K)\)-representation via inflation) as a \(\mathrm{GSp}_4({\mathcal{O}}_K)\)-subrepresentation, then \(\tau\) is isomorphic to the restriction to inertia of the \(L\)-parameter of \(\pi\) (Theorem [•]). This result is essential to our global arguments.

Very recently, Suzuki and Xu proved the explicit local Langlands correspondence for \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) and \(\mathrm{Sp}_4\) [ref]. We expect that one can use their result to extend the inertial local Langlands for more general \(\tau\).

Remark 1 (Transfer from \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) to \(\mathrm{GL}_4\)). We define natural maps sending Deligne–Lusztig representations and Serre weights of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(k)\) to those of \(\mathrm{GL}_4(k)\) (Proposition [•]), which might be of independent interest. They are compatible with mod \(p\) reduction. In the case of Deligne–Lusztig representations, it is also compatible with the inertial local Langlands in a suitable sense. Moreover, this shows that a Serre weight \(\sigma\) of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(k)\) is in the set \(W^?(\overline{\rho}|_{I_{K}})\) of Serre weights associated with tame \(\overline{\rho}: G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\) only if its transfer to \(\mathrm{GL}_4(k)\) is in the set of Serre weights of \(\mathrm{GL}_4(k)\) associated with \(\overline{\rho}\) viewed as \(\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbf{F})\)-valued representation, and the converse holds under a very mild assumption (Corollary [•]). Thus, it seems reasonable to expect that this map respects the property of being modular.

Applications

From now on, we assume that \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified of degree \(f\).

The importance of Corollary [•] is related to the patching argument. Roughly speaking, the patching argument constructs a module \(M_\infty(\lambda-\eta,\tau)\) over (a certain modification of) \(R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\). A standard commutative algebra argument shows that the support of \(M_\infty(\lambda-\eta,\tau)\) is a union of irreducible components in \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}}R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\). It is a folklore conjecture that the support is indeed equal to \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}}R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\), which almost immediately implies a modularity lifting result in a relevant setup. Moreover, it has applications to the Serre weight conjectures and the Breuil–Mézard conjecture. Unfortunately, this is hard to prove in general. However, if \(M_\infty(\lambda-\eta,\tau)\neq 0\) and \(R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\) is a domain, then the support of \(M_\infty(\lambda-\eta,\tau)\) has to be equal to \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}}R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}\). Thus, Corollary [•] together with Taylor’s “Ihara avoidance” argument implies the following modularity lifting result.

Theorem 1 (Theorem [•]). Let \(r,r':G_F \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4({\mathcal{O}})\) be continuous representations that are isomorphic modulo \(\varpi\), unramified at all but finitely many places, and potentially crystalline with regular Hodge type \(\lambda\) and sufficiently generic (depending on \(\lambda\)) tame inertial type \(\tau\) at places above \(p\). We further assume that \(r \bmod\varpi\) is tame at places above \(p\) and satisfies Taylor–Wiles conditions. If \(r'\) is automorphic, then \(r\) is also automorphic.

The geometric Breuil–Mézard conjecture

The original Breuil–Mézard conjecture [ref] measures the complexity of the special fiber of potentially crystalline (or semistable) deformation rings in terms of the mod \(p\) representation theory of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(k)\). Its geometric formulations are stated in [ref] (for deformation rings) and [ref] (for Emerton–Gee stacks) and proven in [ref] in the tamely potentially crystalline case under genericity assumptions. Dotto formulated the Breuil–Mézard conjecture for central division algebras and proved that it follows from the conjecture for \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) [ref].

We formulate the geometric Breuil–Mézard conjecture for \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) in the tamely potentially crystalline case and prove it under genericity assumptions. As a preliminary, we establish the inertial local Langlands correspondence for \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) for a mildly generic tame inertial type (Theorem [•]). For a tame inertial type \(\tau\), let \(\sigma(\tau)\) be the corresponding tame type (i.e. an irreducible representation of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(k)\) over \(E\)).

Theorem 1 (Corollary [•] and [•]). Let \(\Lambda\) be a finite set of regular Hodge types \(\lambda\).

  1. For each Serre weight \(\sigma\), there exists a \(4f\)-dimensional cycle \({\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma}\) in \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{red}}}\) such that \[\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{Z}}_{\lambda,\tau} = \sum_{\sigma} [\overline{\sigma(\tau) \otimes V(\lambda-\eta)} : \sigma] {\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma} \end{aligned}\] holds for any regular Hodge type \(\lambda\in \Lambda\) and any sufficiently generic (depending on \(\Lambda\)) regular tame inertial type \(\tau\).

  2. Let \(\overline{\rho}: G_K \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\) be sufficiently generic (depending on \(\Lambda\)). For each Serre weight \(\sigma\), there exists a \((4f+11)\)-dimensional cycle \(Z_{\sigma}\) in \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}}R_{\overline{\rho}}^\square/\varpi\) such that \[\begin{aligned} Z(R_{\overline{\rho}}^{\lambda,\tau}/\varpi) = \sum_{\sigma} [\overline{\sigma(\tau) \otimes V(\lambda-\eta)} : \sigma] Z_{\sigma} \end{aligned}\] holds for any regular Hodge type \(\lambda\in \Lambda\) and any regular tame inertial type \(\tau\).

By using patching functors and Corollary [•], we first construct cycles \(Z_{\sigma}\) satisfying [•] for regular \(\lambda\), sufficiently generic \(\tau\), and tame \(\overline{\rho}\) (Theorem [•]). Then we algebraically interpolate \(Z_{\sigma}\) for various \(\overline{\rho}\) to construct \({\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma}\) in item (1) following the axiomatic argument in [ref]. Item (2) (where we do not assume that \(\overline{\rho}\) is tame) essentially follows from item (1) by pulling back the cycles \({\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma}\) to a versal ring for \({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathrm{Sym}},K,{\mathrm{red}}}\) at \(\overline{\rho}\).

The weight part of Serre’s conjecture

Let \(F\) be a totally real field of even degree over \(\mathbf{Q}\) in which \(p\) is unramified. Let \({\mathcal{G}}\) be an inner form of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) over \(F\) which is compact modulo center at infinity and splits at all finite places. Fix an isomorphism \(\iota: \overline{\mathbf{Q}}_p\buildrel\sim\over\rightarrow\mathbf{C}\). Given a Hecke character \(\chi: \mathbb{A}_F^\times/F^\times \rightarrow\mathbf{C}^\times\), a level \(U\subset {\mathcal{G}}(\mathbb{A}^\infty_F)\), and an \({\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{G}}({\mathcal{O}}_F\otimes_\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}_p)]\)-module \(W\), we define a space of algebraic automorphic forms \(S_\chi(U,W)\) to be the \({\mathcal{O}}\)-module of continuous functions \(f : {\mathcal{G}}(F) {\backslash}{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbb{A}^\infty_F) \rightarrow W\) such that \(f(zg) =(\iota^{-1}\circ\chi(z))f(g)\) and \(f(gu)=u_p^{-1}\cdot f(g)\) for all \(z\in Z(\mathbb{A}_F^\infty), g\in {\mathcal{G}}(\mathbb{A}^\infty_F)\), and \(u \in U\).

Let \(\overline{r}: G_F \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\) be a continuous and absolutely irreducible representation which is the mod \(p\) reduction of the Galois representation attached to a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of \({\mathcal{G}}(\mathbb{A}_F)\) (or equivalently, of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbb{A}_F)\)). Then \(\overline{r}\) determines a maximal ideal \({\mathfrak{m}}_{\overline{r}}\) of an appropriate Hecke algebra, and \(S_\chi(U,\sigma)_{{\mathfrak{m}}_{\overline{r}}}\neq 0\) for some \(\chi\), \(U\), and Serre weight \(\sigma\). In this case, we say \(\sigma\) is a modular Serre weight for \(\overline{r}\) and write \(W(\overline{r})\) for the set of modular Serre weights for \(\overline{r}\). When \(\overline{r}\) is tame at places above \(p\), [ref] defines a set \(W^?(\otimes_{v|p}\overline{r}|_{I_{F_v}})\) (see Definition [•]) using combinatorial recipes, where \({I_{F_v}}\) denotes the inertia subgroup at \(v\), and conjectures that \(W(\overline{r})=W^?(\otimes_{v|p}\overline{r}|_{I_{F_v}})\). We verify this conjecture under technical genericity assumptions.

Theorem 1 (Theorem [•]). Let \(\overline{r}: G_F \rightarrow\mathrm{GSp}_4(\mathbf{F})\) be as above. Moreover, we assume that \(\overline{r}|_{I_{F_v}}\) is tame and sufficiently generic for \(v|p\), and \(\overline{r}\) satisfies Taylor–Wiles conditions (Definition [•]). Then \(W(\overline{r}) =W^?(\otimes_{v|p}\overline{r}|_{I_{F_v}})\).

Previously, a similar conjecture was made by Herzig–Tilouine [ref] when \(F=\mathbf{Q}\) using étale cohomology groups of Siegel modular varieties instead of algebraic automorphic forms on \({\mathcal{G}}\). We expect that our method can be used to prove the conjecture of Herzig–Tilouine (or its generalizations to totally real fields) if the conjecture on vanishing of mod \(p\) étale cohomology groups of Hilbert–Siegel modular varieties localized at a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal outside the middle degree is known (cf. [ref]).

Analogous conjectures for a rank \(n\) unitary group \(U(n)\) over a totally real field were proven under technical assumptions (when \(U(n)\) splits at places above \(p\) by [ref] for \(n=2\), by [ref] for \(n=3\), and by [ref] for general \(n\); when \(U(n)\) ramifies at places above \(p\) by [ref] for \(n=2\)). For the group \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\), [ref] proved modularity of obvious weights for \(\overline{r}\) ordinary at places above \(p\) assuming modularity of a single obvious weight. See also [ref] for a result obtained by a different approach. Our result is independent of [ref].

Remark 1 (The work of Arthur). We use [ref] and [ref] for the construction of a Galois representation attached to a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of an inner form of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\). These results were proven using the main results in [ref], which are conditional on the twisted weighted fundamental lemma announced in [ref], but whose proofs have not appeared. See also [ref].

Organization of the paper

In §[•], we first recall basic notions related to the representation theory of \(\mathrm{GSp}_4(k)\) from [ref]. Essentially the only new result here is the inertial local Langlands correspondence for \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) in §[•].

In §[•], we introduce local models and prove their properties. Our presentation closely follows [ref]. Where possible, we simplify our argument by deducing results from analogous results for \(\mathrm{GL}_4\). After introducing the global affine Grassmannian and universal local models in §[•]–[•], we introduce mixed characteristic local models and prove the unibranch property in §[•]–[•]. In §[•]–[•], we discuss irreducible components in the special fiber of mixed characteristic local models. In §[•], we classify torus fixed points in each irreducible component under genericity conditions.

We introduce moduli stacks of symplectic étale \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules in §[•], of Breuil–Kisin modules in §[•], and of étale \(\varphi\)-modules in §[•]. Then we bring them together to prove our results on local model diagrams for potentially crystalline stacks (Theorem [•]) and their mod \(p\) reduction (Theorem [•]). Both results rely on the existence of certain local lifts whose proofs are postponed to §[•].

In §[•], we discuss our setup for global arguments and construct patching functors. In the course, we prove a weight elimination result in §[•]. As applications, we prove the existence of certain local lifts in §[•].

Finally, we formulate the geometric Breuil–Mézard conjecture and prove its restricted versions in §[•]. We prove our result on the weight part of Serre’s conjecture in §[•] and a modularity lifting result in §[•].

Notation

Let \(p>2\) be a prime. We let \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) denote a finite field extension with the ring of integers \({\mathcal{O}}_K\) and the residue field \(k\). Throughout this paper, except §[•], we assume \(K\) to be unramified of degree \(f\) over \(\mathbf{Q}_p\). We take \(E\) to be a finite extension of \(\mathbf{Q}_p\) with ramification degree \(e\), the ring of integers \({\mathcal{O}}\), and the residue field \(\mathbf{F}\). We assume that \(E\) is sufficiently large unless otherwise stated. We let \([\cdot]:\mathbf{F}^\times \rightarrow W(\mathbf{F})^\times\) denote the multiplicative lift.

Let \(F\) be a field. We write \(G_F:=\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{F}/F)\) where \(\overline{F}\) is a separable closure of \(F\). If \(F\) is a non-archimedean local field, we write \(I_F \subset G_F\) for the inertia subgroup and \(W_F\) for the Weil group.

Fix a separable closure \(\overline{K}\) of \(K\) and suppose that \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified of degree \(f\). We choose \(\pi \in \overline{K}\) such that \(\pi^{p^f-1}=-p\). We denote by \(\omega_K : G_K \rightarrow{\mathcal{O}}_K^\times\) the character defined by \(g(\pi)= \omega_K(g)\pi\) for \(g\in G_K\). For an embedding \(\sigma: K \hookrightarrow E\), we write \(\omega_{K,\sigma} = \sigma\circ \omega_K\).

Let \(\epsilon\) denote the \(p\)-adic cyclotomic character. If \(V\) is a de Rham representation of \(G_K\) over \(E\), then for each \(\sigma \in \mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Hom}}}_{\mathbf{Q}_p}(K,E)\), we let \(\mathop{\mathrm{{\mathrm{HT}}}}_\sigma(V)\) denote the multiset of Hodge–Tate weights labelled by \(\sigma\) normalized so that \(\mathop{\mathrm{{\mathrm{HT}}}}_\sigma(\epsilon)=\left\{1\right\}\).

Let \(F\) be a number field. For a place \(v\) of \(F\), we let \(F_v\) be the completion of \(F\) at \(v\) with the ring of integers \({\mathcal{O}}_{F_v}\), a uniformizer \(\varpi_v\), and the residue field \(k_v\) of size \(q_v\). We write \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Frob}}}_{F_v}\) for a geometric Frobenius element in \(G_{F_v}\). We normalize the Artin map \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Art}}}_{F_v} : F_v^\times \buildrel\sim\over\rightarrow W^{\mathrm{ab}}_{F_v}\) so that uniformizers are mapped to geometric Frobenius elements.

Let \(G\) be a split connected reductive group over \(\mathbf{Z}\). In the body of the paper, we take \(G=\mathrm{GSp}_4\) most of the time. We write \(B\subset G\) for a choice of Borel subgroup, \(T\subset B\) for a maximal torus, and \(U\subset B\) for the unipotent radical of \(B\). Let \(\Phi^+ \subset \Phi\) be the subset of positive roots for \((G,B,T)\). We denote by \(\Delta\) the set of simple roots. We write \(X^*(T)\) for the group of characters of \(T\) and \(X_*(T)\) for the group of cocharacters of \(T\). We write \(\Lambda_R \subset X^*(T)\) and \(\Lambda_R^\vee\subset X_*(T)\) for the root lattice and coroot lattice. We let \(W\) denote the Weyl group, \(W_a\) denote the affine Weyl group, and \(\widetilde{W}\) denote the extended affine Weyl group for \(G\).

We write \(G^\vee\) for the split reductive group over \(\mathbf{Z}\) defined by the root datum \((X_*(T),X^*(T),\Phi^\vee,\Phi)\). We write \(T^\vee \subset G^\vee\) for the induced maximal split torus. We have isomorphisms \(X^*(T^\vee)\simeq X_*(T)\) and \(X_*(T^\vee)\simeq X^*(T)\). We let \(W^\vee\), \(W_a^\vee\), and \(\widetilde{W}^\vee\) denote the Weyl group, affine Weyl group, and extended affine Weyl group for \(G^\vee\).

We denote by \({\mathcal{O}}_p\) a finite étale \(\mathbf{Z}_p\)-algebra. In the body of this paper, we take \({\mathcal{O}}_p\) to be either \({\mathcal{O}}_{K}\) or \({\mathcal{O}}_F\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Z}_p\) for some totally real field \(F\) in which \(p\) is unramified. Let \(F_p = {\mathcal{O}}_p[1/p]\). Then \(F_p\) is isomorphic to a product \(\prod_{v\in S_p}F_v\) for a finite set \(S_p\) and finite unramified extensions \(F_v/\mathbf{Q}_p\). There is also an isomorphism \({\mathcal{O}}_p\simeq \prod_{v\in S_p}{\mathcal{O}}_{F_v}\) where \({\mathcal{O}}_{F_v}\) is the ring of integers of \(F_v\).

We define \(G_0 := \Res_{{\mathcal{O}}_p / \mathbf{Z}_p}G_{/{\mathcal{O}}_p}\) and \(\underline{G}:= (G_0)_{/{\mathcal{O}}}\). Let \(B\) be a choice of Borel subgroup and \(T\subset B\) be a maximal split torus. We define \(B_0, \underline{B}\) and \(T_0, \underline{T}\) similarly to \(G_0, \underline{G}\). Let \({\mathcal{J}}= \mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Hom}}}_{\mathbf{Z}_p}({\mathcal{O}}_p, {\mathcal{O}})\). Then \((\underline{G},\underline{B},\underline{T})\) is naturally identified with (\(G^{\mathcal{J}}_{/{\mathcal{O}}},B^{\mathcal{J}}_{/{\mathcal{O}}},T^{\mathcal{J}}_{/{\mathcal{O}}})\). The root datum of \((\underline{G},\underline{B},\underline{T})\) is given by \[\begin{aligned} (X^*(\underline{T}),X_*(\underline{T}),\underline{\Phi},\underline{\Phi}^\vee) \simeq (X^*(T)^{\mathcal{J}},X_*(T)^{\mathcal{J}},\Phi^{\mathcal{J}},\Phi^{\vee,{\mathcal{J}}}). \end{aligned}\] We have \(\underline{\Lambda}_R \simeq \Lambda_R^{\mathcal{J}}\), \(\underline{W}\simeq W^{\mathcal{J}}\), \(\underline{W}_a\simeq W_a^{\mathcal{J}}\), \(\underline{\widetilde{W}}\simeq \widetilde{W}^{\mathcal{J}}\), and similarly for \(\underline{\Lambda}_R^\vee\), \(\underline{W}^\vee\), \(\underline{W}_a^\vee\), \(\underline{\widetilde{W}}^\vee\).

Let \(\varphi\) be the absolute Frobenius on \({\mathcal{O}}_p/p\) and its lift to \({\mathcal{O}}_p\). If \(S\) is a set and \(s=(s_\sigma)_{\sigma\in {\mathcal{J}}} \in S^{\mathcal{J}}\), then we define \(\pi(s)\) by \(\pi(s)_\sigma= s_{\sigma\circ \varphi^{-1}}\). When \({\mathcal{O}}_p = {\mathcal{O}}_K\), we fix an embedding \(\sigma_0: K \hookrightarrow E\) and define \(\sigma_j := \sigma_0\circ \varphi^{-j}\) for \(j\in \mathbf{Z}/f \mathbf{Z}\). This identifies \({\mathcal{J}}\) with \(\mathbf{Z}/f\mathbf{Z}\).

We write \(\mathrm{Diag}(a_1,\dots ,a_n)\) for the diagonal matrix in \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) with entries \(a_1,\dots, a_n\). If \(\mu\) is a cocharacter and \(a\) is a scalar, we write \(a^\mu\) to denote \(\mu(a)\). We write \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Ind}}}\) for the unnormalized parabolic induction and \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{ind}}}\) for the compact induction. Any union of schemes or algebraic stacks is defined to be a scheme-theoretic union unless stated otherwise.

We construct a moduli stack of rank 4 symplectic projective étale \((φ,Γ)\) -modules and prove its geometric properties for any prime \(p>2\) and finite extension \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) . When \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified, we adapt the theory of local models recently developed by Le–Le Hung–Levin–Morra to study the geometry of potentially crystalline substacks in this stack. In particular, we prove the unibranch property at torus fixed points of local models and deduce that tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings are domain under genericity conditions. As applications, we prove, under appropriate genericity conditions, an \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) -analogue of the Breuil–Mézard conjecture for tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture formulated by Gee–Herzig–Savitt for global Galois representations valued in \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) satisfying Taylor–Wiles conditions, and a modularity lifting result for tamely potentially crystalline representations. Background Serre’s modularity conjecture predicts that every continuous, irreducible, odd Galois representation \(\overline{r}: \mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q}) ightarrow\mathrm{GL}_2(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p)\) arises from modular forms [ref]. Its refined version predicts the minimal weight of modular forms that give rise to \(\overline{r}\) in terms of the restriction of \(\overline{r}\) at \(p\) . The weight part of Serre’s conjecture, saying that the original conjecture implies the refined conjecture, was crucial for the proof of the conjecture due to Kisin and Khare–Winterberger [ref]. The weight part of Serre’s conjecture has been generalized, most notably, to 2-dimensional Galois representations over a totally real field [ref], to Galois representations over a totally real field valued in \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) [ref] and in more general groups \(G\) [ref]. (Both [ref] and [ref] assume that \(p\) is unramified in the totally real field and the Galois representations are tamely ramified at places above \(p\) . See [ref] for a generalization to wildly ramified representations, and [ref] for a generalization to a totally real field in which \(p\) ramifies.) In these generalizations, the notion of weight is replaced by Serre weights , namely, isomorphism classes of irreducible \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\) -representations of \(G(\mathbf{F}_q)\) . Although stated in the global context, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture is closely related to the mod \(p\) Langlands program. Let \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) be a finite extension. The mod \(p\) Langlands program predicts a certain correspondence between admissible smooth \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\) -representations of a \(p\) -adic reductive group \(G(K)\) and continuous representations of \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{K}/K)\) valued in its dual group \(G^\vee(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p)\) . In this article, we only consider \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\) or \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) , in which case \(G^\vee\) is isomorphic to \(G\) . Such a correspondence has been established only in the case \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2\) and \(K=\mathbf{Q}_p\) [ref] or \(G=\mathrm{GL}_1\) . Despite many recent advances (for example, see [ref]) in the program, its intricate nature remains poorly understood, and a precise conjecture for \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\) was only made recently [ref] in a categorical language. However, using global methods, one can construct a candidate for a mod \(p\) Langlands correspondence, namely, an admissible smooth \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\) -representation \(\Pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(K)\) associated with an \(n\) -dimensional continuous \(\overline{\mathbf{F}}_p\) -representation \(\overline{ho}\) of \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Gal}}}(\overline{K}/K)\) . One major open problem is to prove that \(\Pi\) only depends on \(\overline{ho}\) and not on non-canonical choices made in the global argument. The weight part of Serre’s conjecture describes the Serre weights appearing in the \(\mathrm{GL}_n({\mathcal{O}}_K)\) -socle of \(\Pi\) explicitly in terms of \(\overline{ho}|_{I_K}\) . Thus, the weight part of Serre’s conjecture has been a guiding principle in the mod \(p\) Langlands program. The theory of Galois deformations has played an important role in many advances in proving the weight part of Serre’s conjecture ( [ref]), in the mod \(p\) and \(p\) -adic Langlands program ( [ref]), and in proving modularity lifting results ( [ref]). Recently, Emerton–Gee constructed an object that algebraically interpolates deformation spaces of \(n\) -dimensional \(p\) -adic Galois representations (called the Emerton–Gee stack [ref]). The Emerton–Gee stack allows us to employ more geometric methods to study \(p\) -adic Galois representations. More importantly, it is an essential ingredient in formulating the categorical mod \(p\) and \(p\) -adic Langlands conjecture [ref]. When \(K/\mathbf{Q}_p\) is unramified, [ref] developed a theory of local models to study the geometry of potentially crystalline substacks in Emerton–Gee stacks. In particular, it is applied to analyze singularities of tamely potentially crystalline deformation rings. This led to several applications, including the weight part of Serre’s conjecture and the Breuil–Mézard conjecture. The objective of this article is to generalize Emerton–Gee stacks, local models, and their applications to Serre weight conjectures and the Breuil–Mézard conjecture to the group \(\mathrm{GSp}_4\) . We let \(W^\vee\) , \(W_a^\vee\) , and \(\widetilde{W}^\vee\) denote the Weyl group, affine Weyl group, and extended affine Weyl group for \(G^\vee\) . We denote by \({\mathcal{O}}_p\) a finite étale \(\mathbf{Z}_p\) -algebra. We write \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{Ind}}}\) for the unnormalized parabolic induction and \(\mathop{\mathrm{\mathrm{ind}}}\) for the compact induction. title: On a fully nonlinear elliptic equation with differential forms
abstract_html: We introduce a fully nonlinear PDE with a differential form \(Λ\), which unifies several important equations in Kähler geometry including Monge-Ampère equations, J-equations, inverse \(σ_{k}\) equations, and the deformed Hermitian Yang-Mills (dHYM) equation. We pose some natural positivity conditions on \(Λ\), and prove analytical and algebraic criterions for the solvability of the equation. Our results generalize previous works of G.Chen, J.Song, Datar-Pingali and others. As an application, we prove a conjecture of Collins-Jacob-Yau for the dHYM equation with small global phase.
introduction_html:
In this paper, we study a general form of fully non-linear partial differential equations of Monge-Ampère type on \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) manifolds.

Let \((M,\omega_{0})\) be a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) manifold of dimension \(n\), and let \([\omega_{0}]\) be the corresponding \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) class. We fix a closed differential form of the following format: \[\Lambda=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Lambda^{[k]},\] where for each \(1\leq k\leq n\), \(\Lambda^{[k]}\) is a real \((k,k)\)-form. Hereby we use \(\alpha^{[k]}\) to denote the \((k,k)\) component of a differential form \(\alpha\). Let \(\omega=\omega_{0}+i\partial\bar{\partial}u\in[\omega_{0}]\) be a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) metric. We denote \[\Omega=\Omega(\omega)=\exp\omega=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\omega^{k}}{k!}.\] In this paper, we study the following partial differential equation of function \(u\): \[\kappa\Omega^{[n]}=(\Lambda\wedge\Omega)^{[n]},\] where \(\kappa\) is a positive constant such that \(\kappa\int_{M}\exp\omega_{0}=\int_{M}\Lambda\wedge\exp\omega_{0}.\)

When \(\Lambda\) has only the positive \((n,n)\) component, it is thus a volume form of \(M\). ([•]) is the well-known complex Monge-Ampère equation, first completely solved by Yau [ref].

For future convenience, we write \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) as \(\frac{f\rho^{n}}{n!}\), where \(f\) is a smooth function on \(M\)and \(\rho\) is a fixed background \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) metric. Then ([•]) can be expanded as:

\[\kappa\frac{\omega^{n}}{n!}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\Lambda^{[k]}\wedge\frac{\omega^{n-k}}{(n-k)!}+f\frac{\rho^{n}}{n!}.\]

In addition to the original Monge-Ampère equation, other special cases of equation ([•]) include:

  1. When \(\Lambda=\rho\) is a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) form, ([•]) is the \(J\)-equation, which was first introduced by Donaldson [ref] and has been extensively studied by many authors. See [ref] and references therein.

  2. When \(\Lambda\) is \(\rho^{k}\) or \(\sum_{i=k}^{n-1}c_{k}\rho^{k}\), where \(\rho\) is a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) form and \(c_{k}\geq0\), ([•]) is the inverse \(\sigma_{k}\)-equation, which was first raised in Fang-Lai-Ma [ref]. An incomplete list of works on these equations includes [ref].

  3. Given a specific global phase \(\theta>0\) and \(\Lambda=\sin\theta\cos\rho-\cos\theta\sin\rho\), where \(\rho\) is a Kähler form, ([•]) is the deformed Hermitian Yang-Mills (dHYM) equation. dHYM equation was introduced in Marino-Minasian-Moore-Strominger [ref] and Leung-Yau-Zaslow [ref] and has been extensively studied; See [ref] and references therein. See also Section [•] for details.

PDEs in the general form of ([•]) are inspired by above-mentioned works, which have roots in rich geometric and mathematical physics background, and are important in the field of fully non-linear PDEs with significant geometric implications. Known results indicate that the existence of unique smooth solutions can be interpreted as analytical and algebraic properties of the underlying manifold. Therefore, it is our intention to systematically explore more general forms of such PDEs. In particular, we would like to study necessary and sufficient conditions that ensure the existence of solutions.

We realize from past works that, aside from the unknown Kähler metric to be solved, given geometric data often involve another Kähler form or its powers. The exact format of ([•]) suggests some point-wise positivity requirement for the differential form \(\Lambda.\) In addition, the important fact of ellipticity of Monge-Ampère type equations poses similar requirements. One of our main goals is to find natural positivity conditions under which necessary a priori estimates can be established and deep connections between PDE and geometry can be reconstructed. Inspired by Gao Chen’s work [ref], we also consider ([•]) in a bit more general form, in which we allow \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) to be slightly negative at some points.

For convenience of further discussion, we decompose \(\Lambda\) as follows \[\Lambda=\mathring{\Lambda}+\Lambda^{[n]},\] and discuss constraints on \(\mathring{\Lambda}\) and \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) separately.

1. We call a real even closed differential form \(\mathring{\Lambda}\) on M \(k\)-uniformly positive (\(k\)-UP) if there exists an integer \(1\leq k\le n\), a reference \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) metric \(\rho\) of \(M\), and a uniform constant \(m>0\) such that \(\Lambda^{[l]}=0\) for \(l<k\) ; and \[\mathring{\Lambda}-m\frac{\rho^{k}}{k!}\geq0,\] which ([•]) means that each \((l,l)\)-component of the left hand side is a positive form for \(1\leq l\leq n\). See Definition [•].

Notice that Definition [•] is independent of the choice of reference metric \(\rho\). An \(n\)-UP form \(\Lambda\) is a positive volume form, which is required for solving the classic Monge-Ampère equation. \(J\)-equation is a special case where \(\Lambda\) is \(1\)-UP. Furthermore, positive linear combination of powers of a given Kähler form is uniformly positive. Therefore, inverse \(\sigma_{k}\) equations also fall into this category. However, as uniform positivity is an open condition, it is far more general than these special cases. In future sections, we will also give more general and technical conditions under which various conclusions hold.

Since the classic Monge-Ampère equation is well known in the field, we will discuss only cases when \(\mathring{\Lambda}\) is \(k\)-UP for some \(1\leq k\leq n-1\). When we consider \(\Lambda^{[n]},\) in spirit of the work of G. Chen [ref], we pose a slightly weaker condition.

2. Given \(1\leq k_{0}\leq n-1\), \(m>0\), and a reference \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) metric \(\rho\), we call \((n,n)\)-form \(\alpha\) an almost positive volume form with respect to \((k_{0},m,\rho)\), if \(\int_{M}\alpha\geq0\) and there exists \(\epsilon=\epsilon(n,m,\kappa,k_{0},\omega_{0},\rho)>0\) such that \[\frac{\alpha}{\rho^{n}/n!}>-\epsilon.\]

3. We will choose a specific constant \(\epsilon<\min\left\{ \frac{m}{4n+2}\gamma_{\min}(\frac{2\kappa}{m},1,n,k_{0}),\frac{\kappa\int_{M}\omega_{0}^{n}}{2\int_{M}\rho^{n}}\right\} ,\)where \(\gamma_{\min}\) is a positive number, defined later in ([•]) in the rest of the paper.

We state the following hypothesis on \(\Lambda\), which will be a key assumption for our paper.

4. \(\Lambda=\mathring{\Lambda}+\Lambda^{[n]}\) is called to satisfy the condition H1, if and only if \(\mathring{\Lambda}\) is \(k_{0}\)-uniformly positive for some \(1\leq k_{0}\leq n-1\) with a reference metric \(\rho\) and a uniform constant \(m>0\); and \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) is almost positive with respect to a specific \(\epsilon\)(as in Remark [•]) and \((k_{0},m,\rho)\).

In order to state our main analytical result, we define the following concept based on previous works ( [ref] ).

5. A \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) form \(\omega\in[\omega_{0}]\) is called to satisfy the cone condition for equation ([•]) if and only if pointwisely it satisfies the following \[\kappa(\exp\omega)^{[n-1]}-\left(\Lambda\wedge\exp\omega\right)^{[n-1]}>0;\] Or equivalently, \[\frac{\kappa\omega^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{\Lambda^{[k]}\wedge\omega^{n-k-1}}{(n-k-1)!}>0,\] which means that the left hand side of ([•]) or [•]) is a strictly positive \((n-1,n-1)\) form. We also call \(\omega\) a subsolution of the equation ([•]) or ([•]) if ([•]) holds everywhere.

In order to state our main geometrical result, inspired by the works of [ref], we propose the following numerical positivity conditions:

6. Let \([\Lambda]\) be the cohomology class of \(\Lambda\). Let \(\kappa>0\) be a constant. Let \([\alpha]\) be a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) class. We call \([\alpha]\) a \(([\Lambda],\kappa)\)-positive class if \[[\exp\alpha]\cdot[\kappa-\Lambda]\cdot[M]\geq0,\] and for any subvariety \(Y\) of \(M\) with \(\dim Y<n\) it holds that \[[\exp\alpha]\cdot[\kappa-\Lambda]\cdot[Y]>0.\]

With key definitions ready, we state our main theorems, which consist 2 parts. The first is an analytic criterion for the existence of solution to ([•]).

7. Let \(M\) be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension \(n\) with a fixed Kähler class \([\omega_{0}]\). Suppose that \(\Lambda\) is a closed real differential form satisfying H1. Then, there exists a smooth solution of ([•]) if and only if there exists a smooth subsolution of ([•]).

Special cases of Theorem [•] have been established by Song-Weinkove [ref], Fang-Lai-Ma [ref], Guan [ref], Guan-Sun [ref], Szèkelyhidi [ref], Chen [ref], Datar-Pingali [ref].

8. We also establish the uniqueness result regarding ([•]). See Appendix [•]. In fact, solutions will be shown to be the unique minimizer of a global functional \(\mathcal{F}\) defined in ([•]). We will further explore the variational structure of equation ([•]) in the Appendix [•] and some future works.

9. Following works of [ref], it is likely that Theorem [•] may be extended to Hermitian manifolds, when similar subsolution definition may be established.

Our second main theorem relates the solvability of equation ([•]) to Definition [•].

10. Let \(M\) be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension \(n\) with a fixed Kähler class \([\omega_{0}]\). Suppose that \(\Lambda\) is a closed real differential form satisfying H1. Then \([\omega_{0}]\) is \(([\Lambda],\kappa)\)-positive if and only if there exists a smooth Kähler metric \(\omega\) solves ([•]).

Theorem [•] generalizes several existing works. In the context of \(J\)-equation, G. Chen [ref] proved the equivalence of \(J\)-uniformly positivity and the solvability of the \(J\)-equation; Later, J. Song [ref] reduced the \(J\)-uniformly positivity to only \(J\)-positivity. In the context of inverse \(\sigma_{k}\) type equations, using different methods, similar numerical results have been proved by Collins-Szèkelyhidi [ref] for toric manifolds and Datar-Pingali [ref] for projective manifolds.

While many of past works are raised from strong geometric background, our work aims at a general form of non-linear PDEs of Monge-Ampère type on \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) manifolds. In particular, our equation is one of the few fully non-linear PDEs that involve general differential forms of different degrees. It is hopeful that future works will reveal more geometry of positive differential forms on complex manifolds, which has not been studied much from the non-linear PDE point of view.

As an application of our main results, we study supercritical deformed Yang-Mills equations to get the following

11. Let \(M\) be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension \(n\). Let \([\omega_{0}]\) be a real \((1,1)\)-cohomology class and let \(\rho\) be a Kähler form. Let \[\cot\theta=\frac{\int_{M}\text{Re}(\omega+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{n}}{\int_{M}\text{Im}(\omega+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{n}}.\] If \(\theta\in(0,\frac{\pi}{n-1}]\), then there exists a smooth solution to the supercritical dHYM equation \[\text{Re}(\omega+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{n}=\cot\theta\text{Im}(\omega+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{n},\] if and only if \([\omega_{0}-\cot\theta\rho]\) is Kähler and for any analytic subvariety \(V\) of dimension \(d\leq n-1\), we have \[\int_{V}\left(\text{Re}(\omega_{0}+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{d}-\cot\theta\text{Im}(\omega_{0}+\sqrt{-1}\rho)^{d}\right)>0.\]

For supercritical dHYM equations, the equivalence of the existence of a smooth solution to ([•]) and the numerical condition ([•]) was conjectured by Collins-Jacob-Yau [ref] and confirmed by the work of G. Chen [ref], Chu-Lee-Takahashi [ref], and A. Ballal [ref] under various stronger assumptions. See more details in Section [•]. The original conjecture in [ref] in its full generality does not hold due to counterexamples constructed by Zhang [ref]. However, Theorem [•] confirms the original conjecture when \(\theta\in(0,\frac{\pi}{n-1}]\). Notice that for Zhang’s examples [ref] , \(\theta>\frac{\pi}{n-1}\). It is therefore interesting to find the sharp range of \(\theta\) in which the conjecture of Collins-Jacob-Yau holds.

We make some comments on our proofs.

We have utilized numerous ideas and techniques of existing results, many have been cited above. On the analytic side: We employ Yau’s continuity method which has been successfully used by many to attack Monge-Ampère type and other types of equations. We follow works of many [ref] to derive a priori estimates. We use Szèkelyhidi’s argument to derive \(C^{0}\) estimate [ref]. We use arguments in G. Chen [ref] and Datar-Pingali [ref] to treat almost positive volume forms. The definition of subsolution is inspired by similar concepts in Song-Weinkove [ref], Fang-Ma-Lai [ref], Guan [ref], and Szèkelyhidi [ref]. On the algebraic side: The numerical condition in Definition [•] is inspired by [ref]. We follow G. Chen’s induction method and overall approach in [ref] to tackle the numerical criterion. We make use of Demailly-Păun’s mass concentration technique [ref]. We follow J. Song’s treatment of singular subvarieties [ref].

We have made a conscious effort to examine existing methods and explore their maximal applicability, which has lead us to the current formulation of general equations and proper positivity conditions. As mentioned earlier, our equation includes many existing important special cases. We apply a new set of local notations and carry out detailed multi-linear algebraic computation involving inverse \(\sigma_{k}\) type quantities.

One key component of our proof is the definition of the uniform positivity and the subsequent H1 condition, which ensure that the important concept of subsolutions can be defined and key a priori estimates can be carried out. We would like to remark that the uniform positivity condition can not be used directly to prove Theorem [•]. From the algebraic point of view, proper positivity conditions are required to be preserved under two important geometric procedures which are used to prove corresponding numerical results: the first is a product manifold construction; the second is passing from a \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) manifold to its sub-varieties. The uniform positivity condition can be preserved under the second procedure, but unfortunately it is not preserved under the product manifold procedure. In order to overcome this difficulty, we introduce a more technical positivity condition, called H2, which is a similar but more general version of the H1 condition and will be stated in later sections. H2 works under the product manifold procedure, but does not descend to sub-varieties. We carefully establish all necessary algebraic and analytic results that are needed in our proofs under these technical assumptions by fully exploring the algebraic structure of differential forms. The final write-up is technical but self-contained for the convenience of readers. We believe that our main theorems, Theorems [•] and [•], are cleanest in format, still incorporate all known special cases and will be of most use in future applications.

Another key component of our proof is a new geometric PDE ([•]) on the product manifold, which is simpler and more flexible than the one used by Chen [ref], even in the J-equation case. Under our general setting, the new equation is compatible with proper cone conditions, and still carries essential algebraic information. See Example [•] for further elaboration in a simple yet illuminating case.

There are several future research directions of interest.

First of all, our results may be extended further. The general form of dHYM equations do not satisfy any of our positivity assumptions, while its special cases have been studied successfully. In [ref], Lin also studied the convexity of inverse \(\sigma_{k}\) type equations with some negative coefficients. This may indicate that some weaker positivity conditions may lead to existence results.

Similar to the J-equation and dHYM equations ( [ref]), there is also a proper moment map interpretation of our equation, which involves an infinite dimensional symplectic space. Such point of view is helpful to consider further generalizations and applications. We would like to address this topic in a future work.

From the PDE point of view, our current approach, as well as several important previous works, heavily depends on the continuity method. It is interesting to explore corresponding geometric flows, which has been successfully used in the setting of J-equation and dHYM equations but missing in the more general setting. See [ref] and [ref] for an incomplete list. Overall, the parabolic approach will expose finer geometric information.

From the geometry point of view, as mentioned earlier, one may explore the geometry of properly defined positive differential forms using non-linear PDEs, which will be a new research direction. Also mentioned earlier, some of our results is likely to be extended to the Hermitian setting. This may further open applications in the field of special geometry and mathematical physics. From another prospective, indicated by works of Datar-Pingali [ref], Chu-Lee-Takahashi [ref] and a recent lecture note of G. Chen [ref], one may explore the more restrictive setting where \(M\) is projective. Studies of generalized Hodge conjecture explore fine distinction between \(\rm{K\ddot{a}hler}\) and projective manifolds. Our general form of PDE may be of help.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Part 1, we establish main analytical results of this paper; In Part 2, we prove our main algebraic result. We give more details: In Section 2, we state our main technical analytical results; In Section 3, we describe our local setup and establish proper notations; In Section 4, when \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) is non-negative, we compute variations of our non-linear differential operators and derive its ellipticity and concavity; In Section 5, we discuss the cone condition and related properties; In Section 6, we extend results of previous sections to include the almost positive \(\Lambda^{[n]}\) ; In Section 7, we establish proper a priori estimate and use the continuity method to prove our main analytical results; In Section 8, we set up notations and make technical preparations for Part 2; In Section 9, we initiate the induction argument to prove Theorem [•]; In Section 10, we prove the key mass concentration theorem; In Section 11, we complete the proof of Theorem [•]; In Section 12, we study dHYM equations and prove Theorem [•].

Acknowledgements

We thank Jian Song and Jianchun Chu for helpful discussions. We thank Gang Tian and Xiaohua Zhu for comments and suggestions. We thank Vamsi Pritham Pingali and Ved Datar for their interest and comments that are helpful.
